did_you_know.text: Did you know? Job describes the gulf between human beings and God, saying that if a person wanted to contend with Him, he could not answer even one of a thousand charges.
Did you know? This chapter describes two aspects of God’s greatness: wisdom of heart and a power that no one can withstand.
Did you know? Job portrays God as moving mountains from their place without people even noticing.
Did you know? In his poem, Job mentions heavenly bodies or constellations called Ash, Kesil, and Kimah, as well as the “chambers of the south.”
Did you know? The statement “He does great things beyond searching out and wonders beyond number” emphasizes that, according to Job, God’s deeds cannot be measured or counted.
Did you know? Job says that God can pass by him, yet he himself will not see Him or understand His ways; this highlights his sense of God’s hiddenness and distance.
Did you know? Job presents two possibilities—strength or justice—and argues that in neither case does he have anyone who can summon God and bring Him to court.
Did you know? Job declares, “I am blameless,” yet still feels that his own words could condemn him; the chapter thus expresses the crisis between his sense of innocence and his suffering.
Did you know? Job compares his days to a runner, papyrus boats, and an eagle rushing toward its prey, portraying the swift passing of life and the disappearance of prosperity.

Did you know? Job says that there is no “mediator” between them—that is, no third party who could stand between a human being and God and judge between them—so he feels unable to argue with God as an equal.
